head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `where = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(nums2)}`
Translating values into positions in the other array
Fenwick tree (also called Binary Indexed Tree, BIT): `tree`, `add(i)`, `query(i)`
A structure for "how many inserted positions are below `i`" in O(log n)
Counting smaller items among those already seen
Where the current value sits in `nums2`
We treat `v` as the middle element of a triplet
Values seen earlier in `nums1` that also sit before `p` in `nums2`: possible first elements
Elements before the middle in both arrays
Values after `p` in `nums2` (`n − 1 − p`), minus those already seen in `nums1` (`k − left` of the seen ones are after `p`): possible third elements
Elements after the middle in both arrays
Each choice of first and third forms one good triplet with `v` in the middle
Insert this position for the later values

p: `nums1 = [2,0,1,3]`, `nums2 = [0,1,2,3]`, so `where` maps each value to itself.
The only good triplet is `(0, 1, 3)`, so the result is `1`.

Values after `p` in `nums2` number `n − 1 − p`. Some of them have already appeared earlier in `nums1` (so they cannot come after `v` there). Of the `k` values seen so far, `left` are before `p` in `nums2`, so `k − left` are after it; subtracting those leaves exactly the values that are after `v` in both arrays.

2179.takeaway: Count triplets by their middle value: values before it in both arrays times values after it in both, using a Fenwick tree for the "before" counts.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many times each value appears
A value can be fully paired only if it appears an even number of times

p: Both counts are even, so the result is `True`. For `[1,2,3,4]` each count is 1, so `False`.

blocks.h: Why is the parity of counts enough?
p: Pairs consist of equal numbers, so each value forms its own pairs independently. A value with an even count splits perfectly into pairs; an odd count always leaves one unmatched.

2206.takeaway: Everything pairs up exactly when every value occurs an even number of times.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `for i, c in enumerate(number) if c == digit`
The largest result; since all candidates have the same length, string comparison matches numeric comparison

p: The larger is `"231"`.

Every candidate has the same number of digits, so the first position where two candidates differ decides which is larger, which is exactly how string comparison works. No conversion to integers is needed (the numbers could have 100 digits).

bullets: Time: O(n^2) in the worst case (up to n candidates of length n); a single greedy scan can reach O(n).

2259.takeaway: Try removing each occurrence of the digit and keep the largest resulting string.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: For each first letter, the set of suffixes (the rest of the word)
A shared suffix means swapping creates an existing idea
Suffixes in group `a` that do not exist in group `b`
Words that are safe to move into `b`'s first letter
Valid pairs between the two groups: an idea from `a` and an idea from `b`, both with suffixes that the other group does not have
The two orders `"A B"` and `"B A"` are different names

p: `ideas = ["coffee","donuts","time","toffee"]`: groups `c: {offee}`, `d: {onuts}`, `t: {ime, offee}`.
The total is `6`.

blocks.h: Why only compare pairs of first letters?
p: Swapping the first letters of two ideas that start with the same letter changes nothing, so only ideas with different first letters can form a name. After the swap, `A` becomes `letterB + suffixA`. It is a new word exactly when `suffixA` is not in group B, and the same for `B`. So it is enough to count suffixes by first-letter group.

bullets: Time: O(26^2 · n) at worst for the set intersections.

2306.takeaway: Group suffixes by first letter; for each pair of letters, count suffixes unique to each side and multiply, times 2 for the order.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The largest increase in `sum(a)` that swapping one subarray with `b` can bring
Change in `a`'s sum at one index if its element is replaced by `b`'s
Best gain of a subarray ending here, or start fresh (or swap nothing)
Try improving either array and take the better
The score is the larger sum

p: `sum(nums1) + 30 = 210`. Improving `nums2` instead gives `110 + 70 = 180`, so the answer is `210`.

Swapping a segment moves its elements from one array to the other: one sum rises by the segment's difference and the other falls by the same amount. The score is the larger sum, so we find the best improvement for each array separately; the best segment is a maximum-sum subarray of the differences.

2321.takeaway: Swapping a segment changes the sums by the sum of differences, so run Kadane's algorithm on the differences for each direction.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The faces collected in the current round
Every face has appeared at least once, so every sequence of this length can be formed
Start a new round after a complete one
After `rounds` complete rounds, every sequence of that length exists; some sequence of length `rounds + 1` does not

p: The answer is `2 + 1 = 3`.

blocks.h: Why does a full round guarantee all shorter sequences?
p: Each round contains every face, so after `r` rounds any sequence of length `r` can be picked one face per round. The leftover part after the last complete round misses some face, so a sequence that needs that face in the next position cannot be completed. That makes the answer `rounds + 1`.

2350.takeaway: Greedily cut the rolls into rounds that contain all k faces; the shortest missing sequence is one longer than the number of complete rounds.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many of each digit are available
Half of the pairs of digit `d`: one copy of each pair goes into the left half
Palindromes are built from mirrored pairs
Largest digit first, so the left half is as large as possible
Remove zeros at the front, which would make a leading zero
The largest digit with an odd count can go in the centre
If no usable pairs remain, answer is the best single digit (or `0`)
Mirror the left half around the middle

blocks.h: Why strip zeros from the left half only?
p: The half is ordered from large to small digits, so zeros sit at its end unless nothing else is there. A left half consisting only of zeros would lead to a number such as `00900`. Stripping them leaves an empty half, and then the best answer is just the middle digit, or `0` if there is none.

2384.takeaway: Build the left half from pairs of the largest digits, put the largest leftover digit in the middle, and avoid a leading zero.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) with path compression
Merging connected parts of a graph
Number of nodes in the component that carry the root's value (the maximum value in it)
Process edges in order of the largest value they touch, so a component only ever contains values at or below the current edge's maximum
Adding nodes from the smallest value upward
Two components whose maximum values are equal get connected, creating a good path between each pair of nodes at that maximum value
Attach the component with the smaller maximum below the larger one, keeping the larger value at the root
The root must always hold the component's maximum
Every single node is a good path

p: `vals = [1,3,2,1,3]`, `edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[2,3],[2,4]]`. Edges sorted by their larger endpoint value: `(0,2)` and `(2,3)` (max 2), then `(0,1)` and `(2,4)` (max 3).
The answer is `6`.

blocks.h: Why process edges in increasing order of their max value?
p: A good path can only pass through nodes whose values are at most the endpoint value. When an edge with maximum value `v` is processed, the component of each endpoint contains only nodes with values `≤ v`. Two components whose largest values are both exactly `v` are then joined by a path that stays at or below `v`, so every pair of their `v`-valued nodes gives a new good path.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) (sorting the edges, near-linear union-find).

2421.takeaway: Add edges by increasing max value with Union-Find, tracking how many nodes in each component hold the component's max; merging two equal maxima adds count × count paths.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Merge the components of the two cities of every road
The road belongs to the component of city 1
The smallest road distance in that component

p: `n = 4`, `roads = [[1,2,9],[2,3,6],[2,4,5],[1,4,7]]`: all cities end up in one component.
The minimum is `5`.

blocks.h: Why any road in the component?
p: A path may use roads and cities more than once, so from city 1 you can walk to any road in the same component, cross it, and come back. Since city `n` is guaranteed to be connected to city 1, the best score is simply the smallest edge in that component.

bullets: Time: O((n + roads) · α(n)), nearly linear.

2492.takeaway: Connect all cities with Union-Find and take the minimum road in the component that contains city 1.

The answer is at least the current minimum and at most that plus `k`

blocks.h: Why place stations as far right as possible?
p: When city `i` is short, any new station must cover city `i`. Placing it at city `i + r` covers the furthest cities to the right (`i .. i + 2r`), which helps later cities the most. Since cities to the left are already satisfied, nothing is lost.

2528.takeaway: Binary search the target power; check it greedily from the left, building the needed stations as far right as possible with a difference array.

One array ran out without a match

blocks.h: Why does the first match give the minimum?
p: Both arrays are sorted and the pointers always sit at the smallest unchecked values. Anything skipped was smaller than the value in the other array and so could not appear there. The first equal pair is therefore the smallest shared value.

2540.takeaway: Walk two pointers over the sorted arrays, advancing the smaller one, and stop at the first equal pair.

The cells of the smaller diamond layer
The coloured region is a diamond, which is made of two interleaved squares

p: The number of coloured cells after `n` minutes:

The diamond has rows of width 1, 3, 5, ..., 2n − 1, ..., 3, 1. Colouring the cells in a checkerboard way, the cells of one colour form an `n × n` square and the other colour an `(n − 1) × (n − 1)` square. Adding them gives the whole diamond.

head: Code
Meaning

Pairs (value, index) in order of value, with ties broken by the smaller index
Processing in the order the rules specify
The first unmarked element in sorted order is the smallest unmarked one
Add the value and mark it with both neighbours

p: The score is `7`.

Marking only ever removes elements from consideration. Walking the globally sorted list and skipping marked elements visits unmarked elements in exactly the order "smallest value, then smallest index".

2593.takeaway: Sort the pairs (value, index), take each unmarked one, and mark it with its neighbours.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The sorted list of indices where value `x` occurs
Sum of all indices in the group
Used to get the sum of distances in O(1)
Sum of the indices before the current one in the group
Sum of distances to the `j` earlier indices: each is `i − earlier`
Sum of distances to the `m − j − 1` later indices: each is `later − i`

p: `nums = [1,3,1,1,2]`: value `1` occurs at indices `[0,2,3]`, `total = 5`, `m = 3`.
Result `[5,0,3,4,0]`; the values `3` and `2` occur once and get `0`.

blocks.h: Why this beats comparing all pairs?
p: Instead of adding `|i − j|` for every pair, the sum of distances to earlier indices is `i · (their count) − (their sum)`, and to later indices `(their sum) − i · (their count)`. A running prefix sum makes each of these O(1).

2615.takeaway: Group equal values, and use prefix sums of positions to compute the sum of distances to the earlier and later copies in O(1).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Try each possible number of operations
After `k` operations the `num2` parts have been removed `k` times, so `x` must be exactly the sum of `k` powers of two
`k` powers of two (each at least 1) sum to at least `k`
The fewest powers of two that add up to `x` is its number of 1 bits; extra ones can be made by splitting a power into two halves

p: The answer is `3`.

blocks.h: Why can any count between the number of ones and `x` be reached?
p: A power of two (`2^i` with `i > 0`) can be split into two copies of `2^(i−1)`, which increases the count of terms by one. Starting from the minimum (the 1 bits of `x`), we can reach any count up to `x` by splitting until all terms are 1.

2749.takeaway: After k operations, num1 − k · num2 must be a sum of exactly k powers of two, which holds when its popcount is at most k and it is at least k.

The largest number seen so far whose maximum digit is `d`
`if d in best: res = max(res, best[d] + x)`
Pair the new number with the best earlier one of the same group
Best partner for the current element

p: The answer is `88`.

blocks.h: Why keep only the best number per group?
p: For a fixed partner, the best pair uses the largest other number in the same group. Keeping the running maximum of each group means every number is paired with its best possible earlier partner, and every pair is considered when its second member arrives.

2815.takeaway: Group numbers by their largest digit and keep the maximum of each group, pairing each new number with it.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of elements so far with `x % modulo == k`
How many times each prefix count (mod `modulo`) has occurred, starting with the empty prefix `{0: 1}`
Counting earlier prefixes with a given property
The remainder an earlier prefix must have so that the matching count in between has remainder `k`
Each earlier prefix with that remainder starts one interesting subarray ending here
Counting subarrays by their right end
Record the current prefix for later positions

p: The answer is `3`.

The matching count of a subarray is `pref[r] − pref[l]`. It is interesting when this difference has remainder `k` modulo `modulo`, i.e. `pref[l] ≡ pref[r] − k`. Counting how often each remainder occurred among the earlier prefixes gives the number of valid left ends for every right end.

2845.takeaway: Prefix counts of matching elements plus a hash map of remainders let you count valid left ends for each right end.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: The grid flattened to one list
The answer only depends on "all other elements"
Product of everything before the current element
Product of everything after the current element
Product of the array except self
Keep values within the required modulus. 12345 is not prime, so dividing the total by an element is not possible
Cut the flat list back into rows

blocks.h: Why prefix and suffix instead of division?
p: Dividing the total product by an element only works with modular inverses, which do not exist for every value when the modulus (12345 = 3 · 5 · 823) is not prime. Multiplying the prefix and suffix products avoids division completely.

2906.takeaway: Flatten the grid, multiply the product of everything before by the product of everything after for each cell, and reshape.

p: The question asks for the number of indices, so a value that appears several times counts each time. The set is only used to test membership.

2956.takeaway: Put each array in a set and count how many elements of the other array are in it.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Positions of all horizontal fences, including the fixed borders
`{b - a for a, b in combinations(h, 2)}`
Every possible side length: keep fences `a` and `b`, remove the ones between
Lengths that can be achieved both vertically and horizontally
Square needs equal width and height
The largest square area, reduced by the modulus
No common length means no square

p: The common gaps are `1` and `2`, and the largest square has side 2, so the area is `4`.

blocks.h: Why are all pairwise differences the possible sizes?
p: A field is bounded by two horizontal and two vertical fences that remain. Any two fences (including the borders) can be the remaining ones if all those between them are removed, so each pair gives a possible side length. The side lengths must match in both directions for a square.

bullets: Time: O(h^2 + v^2), at most about 600^2 for the number of fences.
Space: O(h^2 + v^2) for the sets.

2975.takeaway: Collect all gap sizes from pairs of fences in each direction, intersect them, and square the largest common one.
